title: Matrix Exponentiation (Fibonacci)
directAnswer: To get the nth Fibonacci number in O(log n) instead of O(n), write the recurrence as a matrix. The step [Fₙ₊₁, Fₙ] = [[1,1],[1,0]] · [Fₙ, Fₙ₋₁] means applying that 2×2 matrix once advances Fibonacci by one. So applying it n times — i.e. raising [[1,1],[1,0]] to the nth power — jumps straight to Fₙ. Compute the matrix power by fast exponentiation (square-and-multiply): M^n needs only O(log n) matrix multiplies, each O(1) for a fixed 2×2. Read Fₙ off the top-right entry of M^n.

remember.pattern: Encode a linear recurrence as a matrix, then fast-exponentiate the matrix
remember.formula:
M = [[1, 1], [1, 0]]
M^n = [[F(n+1), F(n)], [F(n), F(n-1)]]
so F(n) = (M^n)[0][1]
fast power: M^n via square-and-multiply in O(log n) 2x2 multiplies
rules: The transition matrix `[[1,1],[1,0]]` raised to `n` has `Fₙ` in both off-diagonal entries; read `Fₙ` from `(M^n)[0][1]`.
Use **fast exponentiation** (square the matrix, multiply when the bit is set) — `n` multiplications would be O(n) and defeat the purpose.
Start the result as the **identity** matrix `[[1,0],[0,1]]`, the matrix equivalent of `1` in scalar power.
Reduce **every** matrix entry mod p after each multiply when working under a modulus, and use **long** in Java — entry products of two sub-p values reach ~10¹⁸.
Pin down `F₀ = 0, F₁ = 1` (so `M¹ = M` gives `F₁ = 1`). An off-by-one in the indexing convention is the usual bug; verify against `M² = [[2,1],[1,1]]` → `F₂ = 1`.
whenToUse: You need `Fₙ` (or any linear-recurrence term) for **astronomically large** n — `10¹⁸` — where O(n) is impossible
The recurrence is **linear with constant coefficients**: `aₙ = c₁aₙ₋₁ + … + c_k aₙ₋ₖ`
You want `Fₙ mod p` for huge n in counting / combinatorics problems
Counting walks of length n in a graph (the adjacency matrix to the nth power)
antiSignals: n is small (≤ 10⁶) → the O(n) iterative DP is simpler and fast enough
The recurrence is **non-linear** (e.g. `aₙ = aₙ₋₁²`) → no constant matrix encodes it
You need the **whole sequence** F₀..Fₙ, not one term → iterate once in O(n)
Coefficients change with n → not a fixed transition matrix
remember.takeaway: Any linear recurrence with constant coefficients is 'multiply the state vector by a fixed transition matrix once per step'. n steps = that matrix to the nth power, and fast exponentiation computes a power in O(log n) multiplies. For Fibonacci the matrix is the 2×2 [[1,1],[1,0]], and Fₙ falls out of its nth power. The trick generalises: build the companion matrix of any k-term linear recurrence and you get O(k³ log n).

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you can re-express a linear recurrence as repeated multiplication by a fixed matrix, and whether you know fast exponentiation turns 'apply n times' into O(log n) matrix multiplications.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Multiplying the matrix n times (still O(n)), getting the index convention wrong so Fₙ comes out shifted by one, or forgetting to reduce matrix entries mod p (overflow / wrong residue).
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: Derive the transition matrix from the recurrence, prove M^n holds [[F(n+1),F(n)],[F(n),F(n-1)]] by induction, and note the method generalises to any constant-coefficient linear recurrence via its companion matrix.

problemStatement:
Compute the nth **Fibonacci number** `Fₙ`, where `F₀ = 0`, `F₁ = 1`, and `Fₙ = Fₙ₋₁ + Fₙ₋₂` for `n ≥ 2`.

`n` can be as large as `10¹⁸`, so an O(n) loop is far too slow. Return `Fₙ` modulo a given modulus `p` (Fibonacci numbers grow exponentially, so for large n the answer is always requested mod p).
constraints: 0 ≤ n ≤ 10¹⁸ (use 64-bit for n; O(log n) ≈ 60 matrix multiplies)
Answers are taken mod p with 1 ≤ p ≤ 10⁹ + 7; reduce after every multiply
Entry products of two sub-p values reach ~10¹⁸ → use long in Java
understanding: Fibonacci is a linear recurrence: the next number is a fixed linear combination of the previous two. That means the pair (Fₙ, Fₙ₋₁) transforms to (Fₙ₊₁, Fₙ) by multiplying with one fixed 2×2 matrix. Advancing the sequence n steps is the same matrix applied n times — its nth power. Powers can be computed in O(log n) by repeated squaring, so a problem that looks O(n) becomes O(log n). The matrix's nth power literally contains Fₙ in its entries.

clarifyingQuestions.question: How large can n be?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Up to ~10¹⁸. That rules out the O(n) loop and is exactly why we use the O(log n) matrix power.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Do you want Fₙ exactly or modulo something?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Fibonacci grows like φⁿ, so for large n it's always mod p. I reduce every matrix entry mod p after each multiplication.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Which indexing convention — F₀ = 0 or F₁ = 1 first?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: F₀ = 0, F₁ = 1. With M = [[1,1],[1,0]], M^n has Fₙ at [0][1]; I'll sanity-check M¹ gives F₁ = 1 and M² gives F₂ = 1.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Is this a one-off term, or do you need the whole sequence?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: One term Fₙ. If the whole sequence up to n were needed and n were modest, a single O(n) pass would beat the matrix method.

examples.explanation: F₁₀ = 55. M¹⁰ = [[89, 55], [55, 34]]; the top-right entry is F₁₀ = 55.

approaches.name: Iterative DP (Baseline)
approaches.whenToMention: Mention first — it's the obvious O(n) solution and is the right answer for small n. It anchors the O(n) cost the matrix method beats.
hints: The recurrence Fₙ = Fₙ₋₁ + Fₙ₋₂ translates directly into a loop. What do you need to remember between iterations?
Keep just the last two values, a = Fₙ₋₂ and b = Fₙ₋₁, and slide them forward n times. No array needed — O(1) space.
This is O(n). Fine for n up to ~10⁶, but for n = 10¹⁸ it would take longer than the age of the universe. What lets us skip ahead?
approaches.complexityReasoning: One addition per step, n steps, so O(n) time. Only two running values are kept, so O(1) space. The wall is n itself: when n is 10¹⁸, n iterations is infeasible regardless of how cheap each step is.
approaches.explanation:
Translate the recurrence straight into a loop. Hold the previous two Fibonacci numbers in two variables and roll them forward.

**How it works.** Start with `a = F₀ = 0` and `b = F₁ = 1`. Each iteration computes the next value `a + b`, then shifts the window: the old `b` becomes the new `a`, and the sum becomes the new `b`. After `n` shifts, `a` holds `Fₙ`. Only two variables are ever live, so the space is `O(1)`.

**Why it is correct.** It computes the recurrence literally, in order, so every value is the true Fibonacci number. There's no cleverness to get wrong beyond the initial two values and the loop count.

**Why it does not scale.** The work is one addition per Fibonacci number, so reaching `Fₙ` costs `Θ(n)` operations. That's perfectly fine for `n ≤ 10⁶`. But the constraint allows `n` up to `10¹⁸`; doing `10¹⁸` additions is hopeless no matter how fast each one is. The cost is tied to the **value** of `n`, not its number of digits.

**The leap the optimal makes.** Notice the loop applies the *same* transformation every step — '(a, b) → (b, a+b)'. Applying one fixed transformation `n` times is exactly what raising a matrix to the `n`th power does, and powers can be taken in `O(log n)` by repeated squaring. That observation is the whole speedup.
approaches.insight: The iterative DP is correct and is the right tool whenever n is small. Its only flaw is that its cost grows with the value of n, not its bit-length. The matrix method keeps the same transformation but applies it via exponentiation, so cost grows with log n instead.

approaches.name: Matrix Fast Exponentiation (Optimal)
approaches.whenToMention: The answer they want for huge n. Phrase it as 'encode the recurrence as M = [[1,1],[1,0]] and raise it to the nth power by squaring'.
hints: Write the step as a matrix: [Fₙ₊₁, Fₙ]ᵀ = M · [Fₙ, Fₙ₋₁]ᵀ. What 2×2 matrix M makes that true?
M = [[1,1],[1,0]]. Applying it once advances the pair by one Fibonacci step, so applying it n times is M^n. What does M^n do to the starting vector [F₁, F₀] = [1, 0]?
Compute M^n by fast exponentiation: square M repeatedly, multiply the accumulator by the current square whenever that bit of n is 1. O(log n) matrix multiplies, each O(1) for a fixed 2×2.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Fast exponentiation does at most 2·log₂(n) matrix multiplications. Each multiply of two 2×2 matrices is a constant 8 multiplications and 4 additions. So total time is O(log n) with O(1) space (a handful of 2×2 matrices).
approaches.explanation:
Re-express the recurrence as a single matrix transformation, then raise that matrix to the `n`th power with repeated squaring.

**Building the transition matrix.** The recurrence `Fₙ₊₁ = Fₙ + Fₙ₋₁` and the trivial `Fₙ = Fₙ` together say:

`[Fₙ₊₁, Fₙ]ᵀ = [[1,1],[1,0]] · [Fₙ, Fₙ₋₁]ᵀ`.

Call that matrix `M = [[1,1],[1,0]]`. Multiplying by `M` once advances the state pair by exactly one Fibonacci step. So advancing `n` steps from `[F₁, F₀] = [1, 0]` is multiplying by `M` a total of `n` times — i.e. computing `M^n`.

**Why M^n contains Fₙ.** A short induction shows `M^n = [[Fₙ₊₁, Fₙ], [Fₙ, Fₙ₋₁]]`. Base case `M¹ = [[1,1],[1,0]] = [[F₂,F₁],[F₁,F₀]]` ✓. Inductive step: `M^(n+1) = M^n · M`, and multiplying out `[[Fₙ₊₁,Fₙ],[Fₙ,Fₙ₋₁]] · [[1,1],[1,0]]` gives `[[Fₙ₊₁+Fₙ, Fₙ₊₁],[Fₙ+Fₙ₋₁, Fₙ]] = [[Fₙ₊₂,Fₙ₊₁],[Fₙ₊₁,Fₙ]]` ✓. So `Fₙ` sits at position `[0][1]` (and `[1][0]`) of `M^n`.

**Why fast exponentiation, not n multiplies.** Computing `M^n` by multiplying `M` into an accumulator `n` times is still `O(n)` — no gain. Instead use square-and-multiply: write `n` in binary; keep a running square `base = M, M², M⁴, …` and an accumulator `result` that starts as the identity. For each bit of `n` from least significant, if the bit is 1 multiply `result *= base`, then square `base`. Because `n` has only `⌊log₂ n⌋ + 1` bits, this does `O(log n)` matrix multiplications. Each multiply is a constant amount of work for a fixed 2×2.

**Why start at the identity.** In scalar exponentiation the accumulator starts at `1`; the matrix analogue is the identity matrix `[[1,0],[0,1]]`, which leaves any matrix unchanged when multiplied. It also handles `n = 0` for free: `M⁰ = I`, and `I[0][1] = 0 = F₀`.

**Why reduce mod p and use long.** Each entry of a product is a sum of two products of entries, each entry below `p ≈ 10⁹`. A single product reaches `~10¹⁸`, which fits in a signed 64-bit `long` — but you must take `mod p` after each entry multiplication so it never compounds. Python integers are unbounded, so the mod there keeps numbers small and matches the math.

**Why it generalises.** Any linear recurrence with constant coefficients has a companion transition matrix (size k×k for a k-term recurrence). The same `M^n` idea computes its nth term in `O(k³ log n)`. Counting length-n walks in a graph is the same trick on the adjacency matrix.
approaches.insight: The unifying idea: 'apply the same linear step n times' equals 'a fixed matrix to the nth power', and powers are cheap by squaring. Fibonacci is the smallest non-trivial instance — a 2×2 matrix — but the construction is identical for any constant-coefficient linear recurrence or for counting walks via an adjacency matrix. The reframe from O(n) to O(log n) is purely 'powers can be squared'.

pitfalls: Multiplying M into the accumulator n times instead of squaring — still O(n).
Starting the accumulator at M instead of the identity — off by one power and breaks n = 0.
Reading Fₙ from the wrong entry — it's [0][1] (and [1][0]), not [0][0].
Forgetting mod after each entry multiply — overflow in Java or slow big ints in Python.
Using int for entries in Java — products reach ~10¹⁸; must be long.

edgeCases.behavior: Loop never executes; result stays identity; [0][1] = 0 = F₀.
One set bit: result = M; [0][1] = 1 = F₁.
Every entry reduces to 0 mod 1; returns 0, the only residue.
About 60 squarings — completes instantly, unlike the O(n) loop.

commonMistakes: Using the O(n) loop for n = 10¹⁸ — infeasible.
Raising M by n separate multiplications instead of fast squaring.
Starting the power accumulator at M instead of the identity matrix.
Reading Fₙ from M^n[0][0] instead of [0][1].
Forgetting to reduce matrix entries mod p (overflow / wrong residue).

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Linear instead of logarithmic exponentiation
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Multiplying M into the result n times is O(n) — no better than the loop. Fast exponentiation squares the base and multiplies on set bits, giving O(log n).

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Reading the wrong entry of M^n
commonMistakesDetailed.why: M^n = [[F(n+1), F(n)], [F(n), F(n-1)]]. Fₙ is the off-diagonal [0][1], not the top-left [0][0] (which is Fₙ₊₁). Reading [0][0] returns the next Fibonacci number.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad: return result[0][0]   # that's F(n+1), off by one

commonMistakesDetailed.title: No mod after entry multiplication
commonMistakesDetailed.why: An entry product of two values near 10⁹ is ~10¹⁸; summing two of them without reducing overflows a signed 64-bit long and yields garbage.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad: C[i][j] = A[i][0] * B[0][j] + A[i][1] * B[1][j]; // can overflow long

patternNote: Matrix exponentiation of a linear recurrence. Reach for it whenever you need a single far-out term of a constant-coefficient linear recurrence (or a count of length-n walks) and O(n) is too slow. Encode one step as a fixed matrix, raise it to the nth power by squaring — O(log n). Fibonacci's 2×2 is the canonical instance.
